analysis.one_liner: Gives disabled people a federal right to receive long-term care at home instead of in institutions.
analysis.headline: A long-term care civil rights bill with 224 House cosponsors — including a majority of Democrats and some Republicans — never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal civil right for a person with a disability who qualifies for a nursing home to instead receive the care they need in their own home or community. It tells state governments and long-term care insurers that denying home-based care to someone eligible for an institution counts as discrimination. States would have to write plans to move people out of institutions over up to 12 years, pay home care providers enough to build a workforce, and ensure there is affordable, accessible housing. Individuals could sue over violations, and the Justice Department could enforce with fines of up to $100,000–$200,000.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need help with daily living and qualify for institutional placement but want to live at home; their families, who are currently forced to provide unpaid care or watch relatives be placed in nursing homes; and home care workers, whose pay rates would have to be adequate to support a real workforce.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled people facing institutionalization and their families

how_it_helps.text: Bars public entities (state and local governments that provide or fund institutional placements) and long-term care insurance providers from denying community-based long-term services and supports to anyone eligible for institutional placement, and counts waiting lists, service caps, and policies forcing congregate settings as discrimination.

Requires every covered public entity to submit a transition plan with measurable objectives and annual targets for moving people out of institutions, with implementation within up to 12 years, subject to approval or disapproval by the federal Administration for Community Living.
Makes failure to set adequate payment rates for a sufficient home care workforce a form of discrimination, and requires support programs for family caregivers.

Requires public entities to ensure sufficient affordable, accessible, integrated housing — including funding home modifications — so people can actually live in the community, and to prioritize the lowest-income disabled people.
Requires institutions to regularly notify residents that community-based care is an alternative and to provide it if chosen.

Gives individuals standing to sue for actual and punitive damages and injunctive relief, allows courts to appoint attorneys and waive fees, and authorizes the Attorney General to investigate and seek civil penalties of up to $100,000 for a first violation and $200,000 for subsequent violations.

analysis.who_pays: State Medicaid programs and local governments, which would have to shift or increase spending toward home and community-based care without a new federal funding stream; private long-term care insurers, which are covered by the same anti-discrimination mandate; and nursing homes and other institutional providers, which would lose residents. The bill text creates rights and planning obligations but contains no dedicated federal appropriation to pay for the expanded services.
analysis.who_pays_short: State Medicaid budgets, insurers, and nursing homes

drawbacks.text: The bill creates rights and requirements for states and insurers but contains no dedicated new federal funding stream; states would bear the cost of expanding home-based care and the required housing commitments.
Relief would be slow for many people: transition plans may take as long as 12 years to fully implement, so someone institutionalized at enactment might wait years for the promised option to leave.

The bill defines 'institution' broadly to include 'any congregate setting that is not community-based or that has the effect of isolating individuals with disabilities from the community,' a definition that would be difficult and expensive for states to apply and could prompt years of litigation over what counts as compliant.

States would face federally enforceable civil penalties and individual lawsuits with damages, which critics could argue pressures budgets and courts rather than legislatures to set long-term care policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people affected, the benefit is fundamental: choosing to live in one's own home instead of an institution, which the Supreme Court recognized as the law's goal in Olmstead v. L.C. more than two decades ago. Community-based care is often cheaper per person than nursing home care, so a well-designed transition could save money over time, and the bill gives states up to 12 years and lets them set their own targets. The serious costs are real: it is largely an unfunded mandate on state Medicaid budgets, the housing guarantee asks states to conjure affordable accessible units they do not have, and the broad definition of 'institution' invites litigation. The design is defensible, but the absence of dedicated funding would have been the central fight if it had ever reached a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees — Energy and Commerce and Judiciary — from the day it was introduced, and neither committee held a hearing or sent it to the floor before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 19, 2023 by Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the House Judiciary Committee.
It attracted 224 cosponsors — 208 of the 216 House Democrats and 16 of the 224 House Republicans — a numerical majority of the House.

No further action was taken: there was no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action in the record, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
This continues a pattern for this proposal, which in earlier Congresses was known as the Disability Integration Act; versions have repeatedly drawn broad cosponsorship without reaching a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, nothing changed: state Medicaid budgets avoided new mandates, private long-term care insurers avoided coverage requirements, and nursing homes kept their resident base. People who need long-term care remain subject to whatever their state chooses to provide, and many remain in institutions or on waiting lists.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State Medicaid budgets, insurers, and nursing homes

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the initial bipartisan cosponsor list.

for.name: 16 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Fitzpatrick and Buck, who were among the original sponsors.

for.name: Disability rights advocates, including ADAPT
for.what_they_did: Championed the legislation, which is named for LaTonya Reeves, an ADAPT member from Tennessee who faced institutionalization, and pressed for its passage across multiple Congresses.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no action on it — no hearing or markup — during the two years the bill was pending.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was also referred took no action on it — no hearing or markup — during the two years the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 208 of 216 House Democrats signed on versus 16 of 224 Republicans — and the Republican-led committees that held the bill never scheduled action on it.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and other institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill creates a legally enforceable right to leave institutional care, so every person who moves out is lost revenue for nursing homes, intermediate care facilities, and psychiatric institutions. The industry's interest in the bill runs directly against the people it houses.

States provide or fund nearly all long-term services and supports and would face enforceable obligations to offer home-based care at adequate payment rates and guarantee housing, with no new federal money attached. Their budgetary interest runs against the disabled people seeking care.

The bill's anti-discrimination mandate applies to any entity that funds long-term services and supports, so insurers would have to cover community-based care for members eligible for institutional placement. Paying for more home care raises costs in the short run, though it can also avoid costlier institutional stays.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and direct care workers
industries.note: The bill requires payment rates sufficient to support a workforce, which would expand demand for home care services and improve wages in a sector with chronic shortages and low pay. Workers' and clients' interests point the same way.
